title: Rama grows up
hook: the four brothers; the bow no one can lift

segments.voice: Yesterday: putrakameshti, the fire ritual, and four boys born after the long wait. Today, they grow up, and one of them is asked to leave home.

Four brothers grow up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; so are Bharata and Shatrughna. They learn the scriptures, archery, riding, how to rule. Then a famous sage walks into the court: Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama, who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited so long for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. The family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells him: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher, and he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana follow the sage into the forest. As they walk, Vishvamitra teaches them divine weapons and mantras. They guard his sacrifice and drive the demons off. One demon, Maricha, is hurled far out into the sea by a single arrow of Rama's, and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. Then the sage says: come with me to Mithila. King Janaka has something you should see. In Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself. In Valmiki's telling, it's so heavy it's wheeled in on an enormous iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Kings have come to try it, and in Janaka's words, not one of them could even lift it. Janaka has made a promise: whoever can string this bow may marry his daughter, Sita. Rama walks up to the bow while the whole court watches, and lifts it as if it were nothing. The bow sat there, too heavy for everyone, until the one person whose weight it was walked up. Not simply the strongest man alive: the right person for this particular weight. Some weights are like that: something in a family, a job, a street, that everyone else walks past, and that somehow fits one pair of hands. That's your weight. Tomorrow: what happens when Rama tries to string it.
screen: `INTO THE FOREST WITH A TEACHER.` · `MARICHA, HURLED INTO THE SEA.` · `SHIVA'S BOW, TOO HEAVY FOR ALL.` · `RAMA LIFTS IT.` · then, large: `YOUR WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Ask what weight in your life seems shaped for your hands, something others can't quite carry or haven't noticed: a relative only you can talk to, a skill, a problem at work nobody else understands. Don't pick it up yet. Just notice how it feels to think: this one might be mine.
Vishvamitra, the sage who takes Rama into the forest. Rama leaves home with him, learns to fight, and lifts Shiva's bow in Janaka's court when no one else could.
Your line: your weight. Some bows wait for one pair of hands. Day thirty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. a sage asks for your teenage son to fight demons in the forest. what do you do?
options: offer your army and yourself instead.
fork.reveal: he offers everything but Rama. the priest Vasishtha persuades him to let Rama go, and the journey makes him.

original.note: Sanskrit: bow; the bow of Shiva in Janaka's court.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero is the strongest guy.
what it means: a bow too heavy for everyone waits for the one person whose weight it is.
what a scholar hears: in Valmiki the bow is Shiva's, kept by Janaka; Rama is said to be not yet sixteen when Vishvamitra takes him.

notes: Fresh editor pass (2026-10-01): cut the invented 'waited half his life' and 'first time away from home'; Maricha is hurled into the sea, not across it (Bala Kanda 30); the kings 'could not even lift' the bow per Janaka (Bala Kanda 66), not 'bend'; fixed the garbled 'not the strongest man in the room in general'; cut 'most of us have a bow like that' (told the listener about their life) and the stock turn 'Here's what the story knows'.
'Not yet sixteen' follows Dasharatha's words in Bala Kanda 20; confirm.
The bow's cart: Valmiki describes an eight-wheeled iron cart drawn by some thousands (often read as five thousand) men. Script says 'thousands'. Confirm.
The script splits lifting (today) and stringing/breaking (tomorrow); in Valmiki it's one continuous scene. Confirm acceptable.
